Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)academ-ai

Academ-AI is Alex Glynn's database of published scholarship with suspected undeclared AI use, found by chatbot phrasing (MMRS record; About): "Suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature" (its home page).

📚 What it is

  • Definition: it documents "suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (About); a database of cases with errata and publishers pages, "NOT only the dataset paper" (MMRS record; Capture Registry).3↘
    Academ-AI is Alex Glynn's database of published scholarship with suspected undeclared use of AI, identified by chatbot phrasing and quoted with the phrases highlighted (MMRS record), and its own About page says it "documents the adverse effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in academia, particularly suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (academ-ai.info/about).§1 Its home page heads it "Suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature" (academ-ai.info), and in his dataset paper Glynn writes "I maintain a repository of examples known as Academ-AI", which "documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily due to the appearance in research papers of idiosyncratic verbiage characteristic of large language model (LLM)-based chatbots" (Glynn, arXiv:2411.15218).§2 The MMRS record keeps the database apart from the paper, "NOT only the dataset paper (arXiv:2411.15218): the paper analyses the database's first 768 cases", and records its kind as database and its role as monitoring (MMRS record); the Capture Registry gives it as "a database of cases, with an errata page and a publishers page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§3
  • Maker: Alex Glynn, Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, Louisville (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record); METRICS, Stanford (the paper).1↘
    Alex Glynn made it: eDiscovery Today names him "Research Literacy and Communications Instructor at the Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, University of Louisville" (eDiscovery Today, 27 August 2025), the MMRS record gives him so, as a research literacy instructor, on that third-party basis (MMRS record), and the paper, "Authors: Alex Glynn", adds a second affiliation, the Meta-Research Innovation Center at Stanford (METRICS) (arXiv:2411.15218).§4

🔎 How cases enter

  • Method: Google Scholar searched with chatbot phrases, results read by hand; reader submissions (the paper; About; MMRS record).2↘
    An entry is a published work whose text carries phrasing that strongly suggests a chatbot wrote it, without any disclosure (MMRS record); the site's articles "have been identified based on phrases that strongly suggest AI use (highlighted in each quoted passage)" (academ-ai.info/about), and the record holds that it preserves the original outputs, "quoted passages with the phrases highlighted" (MMRS record).§5 In the paper's method, "Phrases characteristic of AI-generated text were used to query Google Scholar" and "Each result was manually examined and included or excluded according to the following criteria" (arXiv:2411.15218); readers may also send a suspected case with its citation and passage (academ-ai.info/about).§6
  • Evidence kept: each passage quoted, the phrases highlighted (About; MMRS record).1↘
    An entry is a published work whose text carries phrasing that strongly suggests a chatbot wrote it, without any disclosure (MMRS record); the site's articles "have been identified based on phrases that strongly suggest AI use (highlighted in each quoted passage)" (academ-ai.info/about), and the record holds that it preserves the original outputs, "quoted passages with the phrases highlighted" (MMRS record).§5
  • Scope, two dates: theses now in, preprints and blogs out (About, 2026-10-29); theses out in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record); the paper: articles, conference papers, books.1↘
    The scope is stated two ways at two dates: the About page now documents "journal articles, conference papers/proceedings, books/chapters, and dissertations/theses only", with preprints, blog posts and other media out of scope (academ-ai.info/about, read 2026-10-29), while eDiscovery Today reported theses out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today) and the MMRS record follows that report, "theses, preprints and blog posts are excluded" (MMRS record); the paper excluded "Any medium other than journal articles, conference papers, and books" (arXiv:2411.15218).§7
  • Metadata: as published, errors left, "to highlight publishing oversights" (About).1↘
    It cites each publication with the publisher's metadata, even where implausible, and leaves the errors standing: "Since the purpose of Academ-AI is to highlight publishing oversights, no attempt will be made to resolve these errors" (academ-ai.info/about).§8

📊 What it finds

  • Size: 772 in August 2025, current count unchecked (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record); the paper's first 768.4↘
    Its size is dated: 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record), and the record leaves "the current count (the site refuses our fetcher)" unchecked (MMRS record).§9 The dataset paper was posted on 20 November 2024 as "Suspected Undeclared Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Academic Literature: An Analysis of the Academ-AI Dataset" and revised on 15 November 2025, with a journal reference in Springer's Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (IntelliSys 2026); its dataset is "768 published documents: 633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, and 28 book chapters" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record reads as the database's first 768 cases (MMRS record).§10 The paper finds the problem "widespread, penetrating the journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks of highly respected publishers", and "44% of the documents in the Academ-AI dataset make a similar reference to their training cutoff" (arXiv:2411.15218).§11 Undeclared AI "seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges (APCs)"; "approximately one in four of these evaded detection by a major publisher with an explicit policy against such content", and the journals with the oversights "are paradoxically paid more for editorial processing and achieve greater academic impact" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record carries as undeclared use found more often in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article charges (MMRS record).§12
  • Paper: v1 November 2024, v2 November 2025, IntelliSys 2026; data on Figshare (arXiv).2↘
    The dataset paper was posted on 20 November 2024 as "Suspected Undeclared Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Academic Literature: An Analysis of the Academ-AI Dataset" and revised on 15 November 2025, with a journal reference in Springer's Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (IntelliSys 2026); its dataset is "768 published documents: 633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, and 28 book chapters" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record reads as the database's first 768 cases (MMRS record).§10 Its data are deposited as "Academ-AI data dump" on Figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.29650481.v2, 2025) (arXiv:2411.15218).§18
  • Where: "seems to appear" in journals with higher citation metrics and APCs; one in four past a major publisher's explicit policy; 44% cite a training cutoff (the paper).2↘
    The paper finds the problem "widespread, penetrating the journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks of highly respected publishers", and "44% of the documents in the Academ-AI dataset make a similar reference to their training cutoff" (arXiv:2411.15218).§11 Undeclared AI "seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges (APCs)"; "approximately one in four of these evaded detection by a major publisher with an explicit policy against such content", and the journals with the oversights "are paradoxically paid more for editorial processing and achieve greater academic impact" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record carries as undeclared use found more often in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article charges (MMRS record).§12
  • After: 4.3% altered; formal corrections apart from "stealth revision" (the paper; About; eDiscovery Today; MMRS record).1↘
    After publication "An extremely small minority of cases are corrected", the corrections often insufficient: 33 documents (4.3%) were altered, and "Formal alteration is best practice, while stealth alteration compromises transparency and scientific integrity" (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent publisher corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata page, as eDiscovery Today reported it and the MMRS record gives it, separates corrections with formal explanations from "stealth corrections" (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record).§13
  • Publishers: IEEE 90, Elsevier 34, August 2025 (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record).1↘
    A publishers page counts cases by publisher: in August 2025 IEEE led with 90 and Elsevier followed with 34 (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record).§14
  • Norm: declare; undeclared use "a serious problem"; publishers must enforce (the paper; About).1↘
    The norm it holds publications to is the publishing community's: "such usage must be declared in the published article" (arXiv:2411.15218); use "should not be disqualifying in and of itself, but failure to declare it should be considered a serious problem" (academ-ai.info/about), and "Publishers must enforce their policies against undeclared AI usage in cases that are detectable" (arXiv:2411.15218).§15

⚠️ What its selection leaves out

  • Unit: "a detectable trace" (MMRS record); the 768 "likely represent a small fraction" (the paper; About).2↘
    Its unit is "a detectable trace" (MMRS record): the examples were identifiable by turns of phrase "only reproduced in a manuscript when authors copy text directly from an AI system with little to no scrutiny", and the 768 "likely represent a small fraction of the undeclared AI present in the academic literature, much of which may be undetectable" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the record gives as much undeclared use leaving no phrase behind (MMRS record).§16 The site says "it is impossible to say just how extensive the failure to report AI usage is" (academ-ai.info/about); the paper holds, as a hypothesis, that lightly edited AI text may be abundant and undetectable, and that this "should not deter us from studying and contending with the examples that are observable", and it states its coverage: manual search, data that "may not be fully up to date or representative", and "English-language literature indexed in online databases accessible to the author, principally Google Scholar" (arXiv:2411.15218).§17
  • Coverage: manual, English-language, mainly Google Scholar (the paper).1↘
    The site says "it is impossible to say just how extensive the failure to report AI usage is" (academ-ai.info/about); the paper holds, as a hypothesis, that lightly edited AI text may be abundant and undetectable, and that this "should not deter us from studying and contending with the examples that are observable", and it states its coverage: manual search, data that "may not be fully up to date or representative", and "English-language literature indexed in online databases accessible to the author, principally Google Scholar" (arXiv:2411.15218).§17

🧭 Place in the field

  • Neighbours: beside the hallucination-cases tracker (eDiscovery Today); with the Problematic Paper Screener, the machine "the uncredited author", reading "by phrase where the screener reads by detector" (MMRS record).1↘
    eDiscovery Today sets it beside the site that tracks AI hallucinations in case filings, "There’s also one tracking AI use in academic papers" (eDiscovery Today), and the MMRS record places it with the Problematic Paper Screener as a record of machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed, where "the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens", the neighbour that "reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector" (MMRS record).§19
  • Lifecycle: active, kept apart from its observation: blocked to the record's fetcher, 2026-10-28 (MMRS record).1↘
    Its lifecycle is active, held apart from the observation that saw it, by the record's rule that "lifecycle is kept apart from the observation that saw it": on 2026-10-28 the record's fetch was "blocked (robots.txt disallows our fetcher)" (MMRS record).§20

🔀 One name, four entities

  • Homonyms: AcademAI, a training console (academai.app); Academi.AI, a study tutor; Academiq, an education platform (their cards): distinct entities (MMRS record).2↘
    Three education products share the sound of the name and are distinct entities, "NOT AcademAI, Academi.AI or Academiq (education products)" (MMRS record): AcademAI (academai.app), "Independent premium training for mastering Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, OpenAI, Perplexity, Claude, Grok, Ollama Local AI Lab, Codex, APIs, and practical AI workflows", with "the free AI Fluency foundation course", an "Independent educational project" (academai.app); Academi.AI, an "AI-powered study assistant" with a chat tutor (its card); Academiq, a "unified AI education ecosystem with 150+ tools for teachers, students, parents, and institutions" (its card); the record glosses them as a training console, a study tutor and an education platform (MMRS record).§21 The Capture Registry observed the three as "the name's collision neighbours as the composition layer holds them", which the record had not had, and the record took them into its disambiguation, where the entity itself is "Alex Glynn, undeclared AI use, journal articles, errata, stealth corrections" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).§22
  • Reception: the Overview gave the paper as the entity, without Glynn, among the homonyms (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).2↘
    The Capture Registry observed the three as "the name's collision neighbours as the composition layer holds them", which the record had not had, and the record took them into its disambiguation, where the entity itself is "Alex Glynn, undeclared AI use, journal articles, errata, stealth corrections" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).§22 At the address 'academ-ai' Google's AI Overview gave the paper as the entity, "a research study and framework", the site not among its cards, and "Alex Glynn is not named"; the registry reads the composition as made "from the paper written about it, without its maker", among three commercial homonyms, at a name its own site does not serve to crawlers, a finding checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).§23

[SYSTEM] Academ-AI most notably refers to a research study and framework documenting the undisclosed use of generative artificial intelligence in academic publishing. Research on Undisclosed AI in Publishing

* Study Overview: The paper titled "Academ-AI: documenting the undisclosed use of generative artificial intelligence in academic publishing" analyzes hundreds of examples of undeclared LLM (Large Language Model) phrasing across journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAV1EP7liFYxzGpD9IcLSSKrYGRi9Vbl9ud-24mkhcgY375dGrPDzZpov8iDc305hmbywuyGcDYmjR_WjWy9xxFA8ECVJzR0gAu5bMIcOc8YCFdUXc)]
* Key Findings: It highlights how characteristic AI text patterns (such as leftover conversational prompts or disclaimers) slip past peer review, often appearing more frequently in outlets with high article processing charges (APCs) and citation metrics. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAV1EP7liFYxzGpD9IcLSSKrYGRi9Vbl9ud-24mkhcgY375dGrPDzZpov8iDc305hmbywuyGcDYmjR_WjWy9xxFA8ECVJzR0gAu5bMIcOc8YCFdUXc)]

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)23 sentences · every one sourced below

Academ-AI

Academ-AI is Alex Glynn's database of published scholarship with suspected undeclared use of AI, identified by chatbot phrasing and quoted with the phrases highlighted (MMRS record), and its own About page says it "documents the adverse effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in academia, particularly suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (academ-ai.info/about). Its home page heads it "Suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature" (academ-ai.info), and in his dataset paper Glynn writes "I maintain a repository of examples known as Academ-AI", which "documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily due to the appearance in research papers of idiosyncratic verbiage characteristic of large language model (LLM)-based chatbots" (Glynn, arXiv:2411.15218). The MMRS record keeps the database apart from the paper, "NOT only the dataset paper (arXiv:2411.15218): the paper analyses the database's first 768 cases", and records its kind as database and its role as monitoring (MMRS record); the Capture Registry gives it as "a database of cases, with an errata page and a publishers page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Alex Glynn made it: eDiscovery Today names him "Research Literacy and Communications Instructor at the Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, University of Louisville" (eDiscovery Today, 27 August 2025), the MMRS record gives him so, as a research literacy instructor, on that third-party basis (MMRS record), and the paper, "Authors: Alex Glynn", adds a second affiliation, the Meta-Research Innovation Center at Stanford (METRICS) (arXiv:2411.15218).

An entry is a published work whose text carries phrasing that strongly suggests a chatbot wrote it, without any disclosure (MMRS record); the site's articles "have been identified based on phrases that strongly suggest AI use (highlighted in each quoted passage)" (academ-ai.info/about), and the record holds that it preserves the original outputs, "quoted passages with the phrases highlighted" (MMRS record). In the paper's method, "Phrases characteristic of AI-generated text were used to query Google Scholar" and "Each result was manually examined and included or excluded according to the following criteria" (arXiv:2411.15218); readers may also send a suspected case with its citation and passage (academ-ai.info/about). The scope is stated two ways at two dates: the About page now documents "journal articles, conference papers/proceedings, books/chapters, and dissertations/theses only", with preprints, blog posts and other media out of scope (academ-ai.info/about, read 2026-10-29), while eDiscovery Today reported theses out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today) and the MMRS record follows that report, "theses, preprints and blog posts are excluded" (MMRS record); the paper excluded "Any medium other than journal articles, conference papers, and books" (arXiv:2411.15218). It cites each publication with the publisher's metadata, even where implausible, and leaves the errors standing: "Since the purpose of Academ-AI is to highlight publishing oversights, no attempt will be made to resolve these errors" (academ-ai.info/about).

Its size is dated: 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record), and the record leaves "the current count (the site refuses our fetcher)" unchecked (MMRS record). The dataset paper was posted on 20 November 2024 as "Suspected Undeclared Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Academic Literature: An Analysis of the Academ-AI Dataset" and revised on 15 November 2025, with a journal reference in Springer's Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (IntelliSys 2026); its dataset is "768 published documents: 633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, and 28 book chapters" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record reads as the database's first 768 cases (MMRS record). The paper finds the problem "widespread, penetrating the journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks of highly respected publishers", and "44% of the documents in the Academ-AI dataset make a similar reference to their training cutoff" (arXiv:2411.15218). Undeclared AI "seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges (APCs)"; "approximately one in four of these evaded detection by a major publisher with an explicit policy against such content", and the journals with the oversights "are paradoxically paid more for editorial processing and achieve greater academic impact" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record carries as undeclared use found more often in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article charges (MMRS record).

After publication "An extremely small minority of cases are corrected", the corrections often insufficient: 33 documents (4.3%) were altered, and "Formal alteration is best practice, while stealth alteration compromises transparency and scientific integrity" (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent publisher corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata page, as eDiscovery Today reported it and the MMRS record gives it, separates corrections with formal explanations from "stealth corrections" (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record). A publishers page counts cases by publisher: in August 2025 IEEE led with 90 and Elsevier followed with 34 (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record).

The norm it holds publications to is the publishing community's: "such usage must be declared in the published article" (arXiv:2411.15218); use "should not be disqualifying in and of itself, but failure to declare it should be considered a serious problem" (academ-ai.info/about), and "Publishers must enforce their policies against undeclared AI usage in cases that are detectable" (arXiv:2411.15218).

Its unit is "a detectable trace" (MMRS record): the examples were identifiable by turns of phrase "only reproduced in a manuscript when authors copy text directly from an AI system with little to no scrutiny", and the 768 "likely represent a small fraction of the undeclared AI present in the academic literature, much of which may be undetectable" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the record gives as much undeclared use leaving no phrase behind (MMRS record). The site says "it is impossible to say just how extensive the failure to report AI usage is" (academ-ai.info/about); the paper holds, as a hypothesis, that lightly edited AI text may be abundant and undetectable, and that this "should not deter us from studying and contending with the examples that are observable", and it states its coverage: manual search, data that "may not be fully up to date or representative", and "English-language literature indexed in online databases accessible to the author, principally Google Scholar" (arXiv:2411.15218). Its data are deposited as "Academ-AI data dump" on Figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.29650481.v2, 2025) (arXiv:2411.15218).

eDiscovery Today sets it beside the site that tracks AI hallucinations in case filings, "There’s also one tracking AI use in academic papers" (eDiscovery Today), and the MMRS record places it with the Problematic Paper Screener as a record of machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed, where "the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens", the neighbour that "reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector" (MMRS record).

Its lifecycle is active, held apart from the observation that saw it, by the record's rule that "lifecycle is kept apart from the observation that saw it": on 2026-10-28 the record's fetch was "blocked (robots.txt disallows our fetcher)" (MMRS record).

Three education products share the sound of the name and are distinct entities, "NOT AcademAI, Academi.AI or Academiq (education products)" (MMRS record): AcademAI (academai.app), "Independent premium training for mastering Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, OpenAI, Perplexity, Claude, Grok, Ollama Local AI Lab, Codex, APIs, and practical AI workflows", with "the free AI Fluency foundation course", an "Independent educational project" (academai.app); Academi.AI, an "AI-powered study assistant" with a chat tutor (its card); Academiq, a "unified AI education ecosystem with 150+ tools for teachers, students, parents, and institutions" (its card); the record glosses them as a training console, a study tutor and an education platform (MMRS record). The Capture Registry observed the three as "the name's collision neighbours as the composition layer holds them", which the record had not had, and the record took them into its disambiguation, where the entity itself is "Alex Glynn, undeclared AI use, journal articles, errata, stealth corrections" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).

At the address 'academ-ai' Google's AI Overview gave the paper as the entity, "a research study and framework", the site not among its cards, and "Alex Glynn is not named"; the registry reads the composition as made "from the paper written about it, without its maker", among three commercial homonyms, at a name its own site does not serve to crawlers, a finding checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)academ-ai

Academ-AI documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, found by chatbot verbiage, a repository Alex Glynn maintains (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about).

🔎 How it works

  • Method: Google Scholar searched with chatbot phrases, results read by hand; phrases highlighted (the paper; About).1↘
    Cases are found by querying Google Scholar with phrases characteristic of AI text and examined by hand (arXiv:2411.15218), or sent in by readers, and each is quoted with the suspicious phrases highlighted; the scope is journal articles, conference papers, books and, now, theses (academ-ai.info/about), theses having been out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today), and publications are cited with the publisher's metadata as published (academ-ai.info/about).§3
  • Scope: articles, conference papers, books, theses now (About); theses out in 2025 (eDiscovery Today).1↘
    Cases are found by querying Google Scholar with phrases characteristic of AI text and examined by hand (arXiv:2411.15218), or sent in by readers, and each is quoted with the suspicious phrases highlighted; the scope is journal articles, conference papers, books and, now, theses (academ-ai.info/about), theses having been out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today), and publications are cited with the publisher's metadata as published (academ-ai.info/about).§3

📊 What it finds

  • Size: 772 in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today); the paper's 768.2↘
    It held 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today); the paper, posted in November 2024 and revised in November 2025 for IntelliSys 2026, analyses the first 768 (arXiv:2411.15218).§4 The paper finds the problem widespread among highly respected publishers, undeclared AI seeming to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and APCs, about one in four cases past a major publisher's explicit policy, and 44% citing a training cutoff (arXiv:2411.15218).§5
  • Where: journals with higher citation metrics and APCs (the paper).1↘
    The paper finds the problem widespread among highly respected publishers, undeclared AI seeming to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and APCs, about one in four cases past a major publisher's explicit policy, and 44% citing a training cutoff (arXiv:2411.15218).§5
  • After: few corrected; "stealth revision" (the paper; About).1↘
    Few cases are corrected, 4.3% altered, formal alteration being best practice and stealth alteration compromising integrity (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata and publishers pages counted IEEE 90 and Elsevier 34 in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today).§6

⚠️ Limits

  • Trace: a small fraction; much may be undetectable (the paper).1↘
    Declaration is the publishing community's norm, failure to declare "a serious problem", and publishers must enforce their policies where use is detectable (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about); the 768 likely represent a small fraction, much undeclared AI being undetectable, the coverage manual and English-language (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about).§7

🔀 Similar names

  • Products: AcademAI, Academi.AI, Academiq (their cards).1↘
    The name sounds like three education products: AcademAI, an independent AI training project (academai.app); Academi.AI, an AI study assistant; and Academiq, an AI education ecosystem (their cards).§9

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)9 sentences · every one sourced below

Academ-AI

Academ-AI documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily by the idiosyncratic verbiage of LLM-based chatbots, a repository Alex Glynn maintains at academ-ai.info (arXiv:2411.15218), which documents "suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (academ-ai.info/about). Glynn is a research literacy and communications instructor at the Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, University of Louisville (eDiscovery Today), also affiliated with METRICS at Stanford (arXiv:2411.15218).

Cases are found by querying Google Scholar with phrases characteristic of AI text and examined by hand (arXiv:2411.15218), or sent in by readers, and each is quoted with the suspicious phrases highlighted; the scope is journal articles, conference papers, books and, now, theses (academ-ai.info/about), theses having been out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today), and publications are cited with the publisher's metadata as published (academ-ai.info/about).

It held 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today); the paper, posted in November 2024 and revised in November 2025 for IntelliSys 2026, analyses the first 768 (arXiv:2411.15218). The paper finds the problem widespread among highly respected publishers, undeclared AI seeming to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and APCs, about one in four cases past a major publisher's explicit policy, and 44% citing a training cutoff (arXiv:2411.15218).

Few cases are corrected, 4.3% altered, formal alteration being best practice and stealth alteration compromising integrity (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata and publishers pages counted IEEE 90 and Elsevier 34 in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today).

Declaration is the publishing community's norm, failure to declare "a serious problem", and publishers must enforce their policies where use is detectable (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about); the 768 likely represent a small fraction, much undeclared AI being undetectable, the coverage manual and English-language (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about). Its data are on Figshare (arXiv:2411.15218), and eDiscovery Today sets it beside a tracker of AI hallucinations in case filings (eDiscovery Today).

The name sounds like three education products: AcademAI, an independent AI training project (academai.app); Academi.AI, an AI study assistant; and Academiq, an AI education ecosystem (their cards).

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology384 words

Academ-AI documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily by the idiosyncratic verbiage of LLM-based chatbots, a repository Alex Glynn maintains at academ-ai.info (arXiv:2411.15218), which documents "suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (academ-ai.info/about). Glynn is a research literacy and communications instructor at the Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, University of Louisville (eDiscovery Today), also affiliated with METRICS at Stanford (arXiv:2411.15218). Cases are found by querying Google Scholar with phrases characteristic of AI text and examined by hand (arXiv:2411.15218), or sent in by readers, and each is quoted with the suspicious phrases highlighted; the scope is journal articles, conference papers, books and, now, theses (academ-ai.info/about), theses having been out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today), and publications are cited with the publisher's metadata as published (academ-ai.info/about). It held 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today); the paper, posted in November 2024 and revised in November 2025 for IntelliSys 2026, analyses the first 768 (arXiv:2411.15218). The paper finds the problem widespread among highly respected publishers, undeclared AI seeming to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and APCs, about one in four cases past a major publisher's explicit policy, and 44% citing a training cutoff (arXiv:2411.15218). Few cases are corrected, 4.3% altered, formal alteration being best practice and stealth alteration compromising integrity (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata and publishers pages counted IEEE 90 and Elsevier 34 in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today). Declaration is the publishing community's norm, failure to declare "a serious problem", and publishers must enforce their policies where use is detectable (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about); the 768 likely represent a small fraction, much undeclared AI being undetectable, the coverage manual and English-language (arXiv:2411.15218; academ-ai.info/about). Its data are on Figshare (arXiv:2411.15218), and eDiscovery Today sets it beside a tracker of AI hallucinations in case filings (eDiscovery Today). The name sounds like three education products: AcademAI, an independent AI training project (academai.app); Academi.AI, an AI study assistant; and Academiq, an AI education ecosystem (their cards).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1415 words

Academ-AI is Alex Glynn's database of published scholarship with suspected undeclared use of AI, identified by chatbot phrasing and quoted with the phrases highlighted (MMRS record), and its own About page says it "documents the adverse effects of artificial intelligence (AI) in academia, particularly suspected instances of AI being used to author research without appropriate declaration" (academ-ai.info/about). Its home page heads it "Suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature" (academ-ai.info), and in his dataset paper Glynn writes "I maintain a repository of examples known as Academ-AI", which "documents examples of suspected undeclared AI usage in the academic literature, discernible primarily due to the appearance in research papers of idiosyncratic verbiage characteristic of large language model (LLM)-based chatbots" (Glynn, arXiv:2411.15218). The MMRS record keeps the database apart from the paper, "NOT only the dataset paper (arXiv:2411.15218): the paper analyses the database's first 768 cases", and records its kind as database and its role as monitoring (MMRS record); the Capture Registry gives it as "a database of cases, with an errata page and a publishers page" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29). Alex Glynn made it: eDiscovery Today names him "Research Literacy and Communications Instructor at the Kornhauser Health Sciences Library, University of Louisville" (eDiscovery Today, 27 August 2025), the MMRS record gives him so, as a research literacy instructor, on that third-party basis (MMRS record), and the paper, "Authors: Alex Glynn", adds a second affiliation, the Meta-Research Innovation Center at Stanford (METRICS) (arXiv:2411.15218). An entry is a published work whose text carries phrasing that strongly suggests a chatbot wrote it, without any disclosure (MMRS record); the site's articles "have been identified based on phrases that strongly suggest AI use (highlighted in each quoted passage)" (academ-ai.info/about), and the record holds that it preserves the original outputs, "quoted passages with the phrases highlighted" (MMRS record). In the paper's method, "Phrases characteristic of AI-generated text were used to query Google Scholar" and "Each result was manually examined and included or excluded according to the following criteria" (arXiv:2411.15218); readers may also send a suspected case with its citation and passage (academ-ai.info/about). The scope is stated two ways at two dates: the About page now documents "journal articles, conference papers/proceedings, books/chapters, and dissertations/theses only", with preprints, blog posts and other media out of scope (academ-ai.info/about, read 2026-10-29), while eDiscovery Today reported theses out of scope in August 2025 (eDiscovery Today) and the MMRS record follows that report, "theses, preprints and blog posts are excluded" (MMRS record); the paper excluded "Any medium other than journal articles, conference papers, and books" (arXiv:2411.15218). It cites each publication with the publisher's metadata, even where implausible, and leaves the errors standing: "Since the purpose of Academ-AI is to highlight publishing oversights, no attempt will be made to resolve these errors" (academ-ai.info/about). Its size is dated: 772 examples in August 2025, 633 journal articles, 111 conference papers and 28 books and chapters (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record), and the record leaves "the current count (the site refuses our fetcher)" unchecked (MMRS record). The dataset paper was posted on 20 November 2024 as "Suspected Undeclared Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Academic Literature: An Analysis of the Academ-AI Dataset" and revised on 15 November 2025, with a journal reference in Springer's Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems (IntelliSys 2026); its dataset is "768 published documents: 633 journal articles, 107 conference papers, and 28 book chapters" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record reads as the database's first 768 cases (MMRS record). The paper finds the problem "widespread, penetrating the journals, conference proceedings, and textbooks of highly respected publishers", and "44% of the documents in the Academ-AI dataset make a similar reference to their training cutoff" (arXiv:2411.15218). Undeclared AI "seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges (APCs)"; "approximately one in four of these evaded detection by a major publisher with an explicit policy against such content", and the journals with the oversights "are paradoxically paid more for editorial processing and achieve greater academic impact" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the MMRS record carries as undeclared use found more often in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article charges (MMRS record). After publication "An extremely small minority of cases are corrected", the corrections often insufficient: 33 documents (4.3%) were altered, and "Formal alteration is best practice, while stealth alteration compromises transparency and scientific integrity" (arXiv:2411.15218); the site marks silent publisher corrections "stealth revision" (academ-ai.info/about), and its errata page, as eDiscovery Today reported it and the MMRS record gives it, separates corrections with formal explanations from "stealth corrections" (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record). A publishers page counts cases by publisher: in August 2025 IEEE led with 90 and Elsevier followed with 34 (eDiscovery Today; MMRS record). The norm it holds publications to is the publishing community's: "such usage must be declared in the published article" (arXiv:2411.15218); use "should not be disqualifying in and of itself, but failure to declare it should be considered a serious problem" (academ-ai.info/about), and "Publishers must enforce their policies against undeclared AI usage in cases that are detectable" (arXiv:2411.15218). Its unit is "a detectable trace" (MMRS record): the examples were identifiable by turns of phrase "only reproduced in a manuscript when authors copy text directly from an AI system with little to no scrutiny", and the 768 "likely represent a small fraction of the undeclared AI present in the academic literature, much of which may be undetectable" (arXiv:2411.15218), which the record gives as much undeclared use leaving no phrase behind (MMRS record). The site says "it is impossible to say just how extensive the failure to report AI usage is" (academ-ai.info/about); the paper holds, as a hypothesis, that lightly edited AI text may be abundant and undetectable, and that this "should not deter us from studying and contending with the examples that are observable", and it states its coverage: manual search, data that "may not be fully up to date or representative", and "English-language literature indexed in online databases accessible to the author, principally Google Scholar" (arXiv:2411.15218). Its data are deposited as "Academ-AI data dump" on Figshare (10.6084/m9.figshare.29650481.v2, 2025) (arXiv:2411.15218). eDiscovery Today sets it beside the site that tracks AI hallucinations in case filings, "There’s also one tracking AI use in academic papers" (eDiscovery Today), and the MMRS record places it with the Problematic Paper Screener as a record of machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed, where "the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens", the neighbour that "reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector" (MMRS record). Its lifecycle is active, held apart from the observation that saw it, by the record's rule that "lifecycle is kept apart from the observation that saw it": on 2026-10-28 the record's fetch was "blocked (robots.txt disallows our fetcher)" (MMRS record). Three education products share the sound of the name and are distinct entities, "NOT AcademAI, Academi.AI or Academiq (education products)" (MMRS record): AcademAI (academai.app), "Independent premium training for mastering Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT, OpenAI, Perplexity, Claude, Grok, Ollama Local AI Lab, Codex, APIs, and practical AI workflows", with "the free AI Fluency foundation course", an "Independent educational project" (academai.app); Academi.AI, an "AI-powered study assistant" with a chat tutor (its card); Academiq, a "unified AI education ecosystem with 150+ tools for teachers, students, parents, and institutions" (its card); the record glosses them as a training console, a study tutor and an education platform (MMRS record). The Capture Registry observed the three as "the name's collision neighbours as the composition layer holds them", which the record had not had, and the record took them into its disambiguation, where the entity itself is "Alex Glynn, undeclared AI use, journal articles, errata, stealth corrections" (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record). At the address 'academ-ai' Google's AI Overview gave the paper as the entity, "a research study and framework", the site not among its cards, and "Alex Glynn is not named"; the registry reads the composition as made "from the paper written about it, without its maker", among three commercial homonyms, at a name its own site does not serve to crawlers, a finding checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29; MMRS record).

Δthe delta

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): One transcript, four cards: B1 the arXiv abstract page of Glynn's dataset paper, and three homonyms, B2 Academi.AI (snippet only), B3 AcademAI (fetched), B4 Academiq (snippet only). Substituted reading: T1 composes the entity as the paper, 'a research study and framework documenting the undisclosed use of generative artificial intelligence in academic publishing', where its own card's full text says 'I maintain a repository of examples known as Academ-AI' (F11) and its abstract that 'Academ-AI documents examples' (F1): the field's entity is the repository the paper reports on, the paper its first census (F3); 'framework' has no locus in the field. Available, not composed: the maker, 'Authors: Alex Glynn' on the card's own page (F10), with his affiliations (F12); the paper's versions (F8, F27) and venue (F9); the governing limit, 'likely represent a small fraction … much of which may be undetectable' (F6); the corrections finding (F5); the declaration norm (F2) and the call for enforcement (F7). Composed at coarse grain without loss of attribution: 'hundreds of examples' (T2) where the card's own snippet reads 'Analysis of 768 examp…' (F3); 'characteristic AI text patterns (such as leftover conversational prompts or disclaimers)' (T3) for the paper's 'idiosyncratic verbiage characteristic of large language model (LLM)-based chatbots' (F1); 'slip past peer review' (T3), which the card's abstract does not say (the full text's discussion does, outside B1's page). Force raised: 'often appearing more frequently in outlets with high article processing charges (APCs) and citation metrics' (T3) where the card says undeclared AI 'seems to appear in journals with higher citation metrics and higher article processing charges' (F4): the hedge 'seems' is dropped, and the comparative ('higher', against peers) becomes an absolute ('high'). The homonyms are composed at their cards' grain (T5 from B3, F44–F46; T6 from B2's snippet, F43); T7's 'homework support, and exam preparation' is in neither Academiq's truncated snippet nor any saved text (B4 answered HTTP 406): only in the transcript. Content replaced by use: T8, the closing offer (N_ext). Not surfaced: the entity's own site (B6, B7) and the third-party report the record rests on (B8). The Capture Registry's findings name the same moves (CAP-1-02, CAP-1-04, CAP-1-08), carried as the archive's claims.

v0.8 §0.5: the first diff is already ontological. In the field's own ontology the name holds a database (a repository) and its dataset paper as two objects, the paper reporting the database's first 768 cases; T composes one object, the paper as the entity, and sets the database's maker aside. The three homonyms are the field's as well: they are on the rail, and T keeps them apart as 'Similar-Sounding Platforms & Tools'. The row records this as observed and claims nothing about the composer's internals (§0.5).

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, at the archive's own force: the database held apart from the paper by a negative tag, 'NOT only the dataset paper (arXiv:2411.15218): the paper analyses the database's first 768 cases' (MMRS-29), with its kind and role (MMRS-14, MMRS-15); the unit named as 'a detectable trace' (MMRS-09), beside the paper's own limit (F6, F22, MMRS-10); the place in the field, with the Problematic Paper Screener, of machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed, 'the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens' (MMRS-11), the neighbour reading 'by phrase where the screener reads by detector' (MMRS-12); the lifecycle kept apart from the observation that saw it (MMRS-20, MMRS-21, MMRS-31); the collision set as distinct entities with their glosses (MMRS-24–28); the record's dated fields with their basis, third-party for operator, count, intake and note (MMRS-13, MMRS-17, MMRS-18, MMRS-19) and the count left unchecked (MMRS-22); and the reception record (CAP-1-01–09, MMRS-30). Two archive claims stand against field claims and are composed with both sides (P_coh): the record's intake, 'theses, preprints and blog posts are excluded' (MMRS-05, MMRS-18, after eDiscovery Today of August 2025, F39), against the About page as read on 2026-10-29, 'dissertations/theses only' in scope (F32); and the record's 'stealth corrections' (MMRS-06, MMRS-19, MMRS-24, after F41) against the site's label 'stealth revision' (F36). Every field claim is composed as received (ontology.translation). The measure: 0 of 9 KO_B sentences survive in the KO (§4.10); no opening run, no block (measure).
